title: Tidy Tuesday Analysis
text:
This TidyTuesday dataset is about the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina, Italy. The dataset contains detailed information about all 1,866 Olympic events, including both competition and training sessions across various winter sport disciplines.


Code
olympics_ski <- olympics |>
    filter(str_detect(discipline_name,"Skiing"))

#filtering dataset for sports that are related to skiing only




Code
olympics_ski <- olympics_ski |>
  mutate(medal = if_else(is_medal_event == TRUE, "Medal", "Non-medal"))




Code
# segmented bar chart
ggplot(olympics_ski, aes(x = discipline_name, fill = medal)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    x = "Type of Ski Sport",
    y = "Proportion of Medal Events",
    title = "Proportion of Medal Events for Olympic Ski Sports"
)











Code
# Create new variable for game duration in minutes

olympics <- olympics |>
  mutate(duration = as.numeric(end_time - start_time) / 60)




Code
# scatter plot
ggplot(olympics, aes(x = discipline_name, y = duration)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Olympic Sport",
    y = "Duration of Game (mins)",
    title = "Duration of each game for each olympic sport") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: Eco Tourism
text:
This TidyTuesday dataset is about ecotourism, specifically involving ecological observation and weather condition alongside tourism data.
Credits for data source: Github Link
Nicola Rennie curated the dataset


Code
#Change the year variable to characters (to show full integers, not decimals)

tourism <- tourism|>
  mutate(year = as.character(year))




Code
#Bar plot of number of visits per visit type annually

ggplot(tourism, aes(x = year,y = trips, color = purpose)) +
geom_col() +
labs(
x = "Year",
y = "Number of overnight trips (thousands)",
color = "Purpose",
title = "Tourist visits to Australia",
)









The bar plot illustrates the number of overnight visits people made to Australia each year, categorized by the type of trip being either a business or holiday. The significant drop in total number of overnight trips in 2020 and 2021 is most probably due to COVID 19 travel regulations, and it is seen that as countries recovered from the pandemic, boarders opened up and travel increased significantly in 2022.
Overall, the majority of visits to Australia seem to be for holiday, although there was also a growing number of business trips between 2014-2019. Australia also has a working holiday visa which allows foreigners to work for up to a year, which might be adding to the business category (although it is unclear if a “working holiday” visa is classified as business or holiday).

title: Olympics 2026
text:
This TidyTuesday dataset is about the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina, Italy. The dataset contains detailed information about all 1,866 Olympic events, including both competition and training sessions across various winter sport disciplines.
The data frame combines data from three sources: Olympics.com - Official detailed daily schedule (events, times, venues) Wikipedia - Competition schedule overview table Kaggle - Venue information dataset
Credits for data source: Github Link
@chendaniely, Daniel Chen, curated the dataset


Code
olympics_ski <- olympics |>
    filter(str_detect(discipline_name,"Skiing"))

#filtering dataset for sports that are related to skiing only




Code
olympics_ski <- olympics_ski |>
  mutate(medal = if_else(is_medal_event == TRUE, "Medal", "Non-medal"))

#mutating the is_medal_event variable to show actual description of medal game status




Code
# segmented bar chart
ggplot(olympics_ski, aes(x = discipline_name, fill = medal)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(
    x = "Type of Ski Sport",
    y = "Proportion of Medal Events",
    title = "Proportion of Medal Events for Olympic Ski Sports"
)









This bar chart illustrates the proportion of ski-related Olympic sports that were medal vs non-medal in the 2026 Winter Olympics. Both Alpine Skiing and Cross-Country Skiing are judged strictly by clock time, while Freestyle Skiing involves a mix of timed racing and subjective judge scoring. It is clear that Cross-Country Skiing has proportionately the most medal games, while Freestyle Skiing has the smallest proportion, which might be influenced by the fact that there is a degree of subjective judgement required, hence a team of qualified judges are needed for a medal game.


Code
# Create new variable for game duration in minutes

olympics <- olympics |>
  mutate(duration = as.numeric(end_time - start_time) / 60)




Code
# scatter plot
ggplot(olympics, aes(x = discipline_name, y = duration)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Olympic Sport",
    y = "Duration of Game (mins)",
    title = "Duration of each game for each olympic sport") +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))









The scatterplot illustrates the duration of each game (in minutes) for each 2026 Winter Olympic sport. Figure skating seems to have games with the longest game time at maximum 250 minutes (around 3 hours) and sports that are strictly judged by speed and time, such as Cross-Country Skiing, Speed Skating, or Short Track Speed Skating have the shortest games.

title: Netflix String Analysis
text:
A practice project to understand and experiment str() and fct() functions and various data visualizations in R using a Netflix movie and TV show dataset from Tidy Tuesday.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(openintro)


This Netflix data is from the Tidy Tuesday on 2021-04-20, obtained from Kaggle with credit to Shivam Bansal. The dataset was collected from Flixable, a third-party Netflix search engine. Data includes TV shows and movies added onto Netflix from 2019 onwards (although actual movie release year dates back to 1925), inclduing information such as show title, director, cast, country, release year, and rating.
Credits for data source: Github Link
Checking the first few rows of the Netflix data set below:


Code
# Read in data from Tidy Tuesday
netflix_titles <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2021/2021-04-20/netflix_titles.csv')

#Check first few rows
head(netflix_titles)


# A tibble: 6 × 12
  show_id type    title director    cast  country date_added release_year rating
  <chr>   <chr>   <chr> <chr>       <chr> <chr>   <chr>             <dbl> <chr> 
1 s1      TV Show 3%    <NA>        João… Brazil  August 14…         2020 TV-MA 
2 s2      Movie   7:19  Jorge Mich… Demi… Mexico  December …         2016 TV-MA 
3 s3      Movie   23:59 Gilbert Ch… Tedd… Singap… December …         2011 R     
4 s4      Movie   9     Shane Acker Elij… United… November …         2009 PG-13 
5 s5      Movie   21    Robert Luk… Jim … United… January 1…         2008 PG-13 
6 s6      TV Show 46    Serdar Akar Erda… Turkey  July 1, 2…         2016 TV-MA 
# ℹ 3 more variables: duration <chr>, listed_in <chr>, description <chr>


Given the information available on the Netflix data set, here are some questions of interest that we can explore:

What are the most common movie and TV show genres represented in Netflix?
Out of the movies on Netflix, which is the most common rating (maturity) and is there a pattern among certain genres?
How has the distribution of movie running times (mins) changed over the years, from 1925 to 2021?

Code to clean the data


Code
# Clean data to create new string variable that shows movie/ tv show genre 

table(netflix_titles$rating)



       G    NC-17       NR       PG    PG-13        R    TV-14     TV-G 
      39        3       84      247      386      665     1931      194 
   TV-MA    TV-PG     TV-Y    TV-Y7 TV-Y7-FV       UR 
    2863      806      280      271        6        5 


Code
netflix_titles <- netflix_titles |>
  mutate(rating = fct_relevel(rating, c("NR", "UR", "TV-Y", "TV-Y7", "TV-Y7-FV", "G", "TV-G", "PG", "TV-PG", "PG-13", "TV-14", "R", "TV-MA", "NC-17")))

#NR = not rated
#UR = unrated
#TV-Y7-FV = a sub category of TV-Y7 

netflix_titles <- netflix_titles |>
    mutate(genre = str_extract(listed_in,"^[^,]+"))|>
    mutate(genre2 = str_extract(listed_in,"(?<=, )[^,]+"))|>
    mutate(genre3 = str_match(listed_in,"^[^,]+, [^,]+, ([^,]+)")[, 2])




Code
# Create two separate data frames for movies only, because I want to analyse it separately
netflix_movies <- netflix_titles |> 
  filter(type == "Movie")|>
  mutate(duration = as.integer(str_remove(duration," min$")))




Code
#Create a dataframe for only netflix movies

netflix_movies <- netflix_titles |> 
  filter(type == "Movie")|>
  mutate(duration = as.integer(str_remove(duration," min$")))

#table(netflix_movies$genre)

#Group a few genres together that are more niche
netflix_movies <- netflix_movies |>
    mutate(genre_summary=fct_collapse(genre,
    "Horror & Thriller"= c("Horror Movies", "Thrillers"),
    Comedy= c("Stand-Up Comedy", "Comedies"),
    Other= c("LGBTQ Movies","Sports Movies","Music & Musicals","Romantic Movies","Independent Movies","Cult Movies"),
    "NA" = "Movies")) |>
        filter(genre_summary != "NA")

#Relevel factor by count

netflix_titles <- netflix_titles |>
  mutate(rating = fct_relevel(rating, c("NR", "UR", "TV-Y", "TV-Y7", "TV-Y7-FV", "G", "TV-G", "PG", "TV-PG", "PG-13", "TV-14", "R", "TV-MA", "NC-17")))

#table(netflix_movies$genre_summary)




Code
#Create bar chart showing what movie genres are common
netflix_movies|>
    mutate(genre_summary = fct_infreq(genre_summary))|>
    ggplot(aes(x = genre_summary)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(
        x = "Movie Genre",
        y = "Count",
        title = "Netflix Movie Genres",
        subtitle = "Movies added on Netflix since 2019"
        ) +
            theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))









The bar graph above illustrates the most common types of movie genres represented on Netflix since 2019. Comedy, which includes both comedy shows and stand-up comedy, and dramas seem to be the most common, exceeding a count of 1500 movies for each category. Outside of the (understandable) popularity of Netflix comedy movies online and on social media being a justification for this high count, it is also possible that other sub-genres of comedy, such as romantic comedy (eg. “The Kissing Booth”), satire, and dark/ black comedy (eg. “Don’t Look Up”) are also included in the broad genre. Documentaries and Action & Adventure are the second most popular genres, followed by Children & Family movies.
A few caveats to the visualization is that each movie had multiple genre categories (up to 3) they belonged to and only the first identified genre was used to classify the movie. Also, less common genres, including LGBTQ Movies, Sports Movies, Music & Musicals, Romantic Movies, Independent Movies, and Cult Movies were grouped into “Other,” which means that the number of movies in each of these individual niches could be a much smaller number.


Code
#Create bar chart showing what maturity ratings are common
netflix_movies|>
    ggplot(aes(x = rating)) +
    geom_bar() +
    labs(
        x = "Movie Maturity Rating",
        y = "Count",
        title = "Netflix Movie Maturity Ratings",
        subtitle = "Movies added on Netflix since 2019"
        ) +
            theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))









The bar chart above displays the matury ratings of movies on Netflix (specifically movies added onto Netflix from 2019 onwards). NR is “Not Rated” and UR is “Unrated,” but other than those two categories the rest of the ratings are displayed from the lowest (for youngest children) to the highest (for older teens and adults only). Refer to github source for more information on each maturity rating.
It is clear from the bar chart that there is a larger number of movies that have a more mature rating that requires parental guidance or are for adults only, with Mature Audience Only (TV-MA) being the most popular. However, from this visualization it is impossible to see which specific types of movies are often categorized into a certain maturity rating.


Code
#Create heatmap showing what maturity ratings are common for what genre

netflix_movies |>
  count(genre_summary, rating) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rating, y = genre_summary, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), color = "white", size = 3) +
    labs(
        x = "Movie Maturity Rating",
        y = "Movie Genre",
        title = "Netflix Movie Maturity Ratings for each Genre",
        subtitle = "Movies added on Netflix since 2019"
        ) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))









While the previous bar graph did not provide any information about the relationship between maturity rating and movie genre, this heatmap shows how many of each movie genre is categorized as a specific rating.
From the heatmap colors, the variable that stands out the most is Comedy, with 622 comedy movies being rated “Mature Audience Only” and 384 movies as “Parents Strongly Cautioned.” This makes sense because comedy can often be more vulgular and involve inappropriate or mature jokes. Dramas also have 537 movies that are TV-MA, followed by 374 rated TV-14 and 214 as R-rated. Again, given the often sensitive, mature, and possibly sexual topics that drama movies have, this distribution of rating makes sense.
What interested me is that 281 documentaries are rated TV-MA. Because I don’t watch documentaries, it makes me wonder what topics result in a mature rating for these movies because documentaries often remind me of nature shows, food documentaries, and travel documentaries.
